evidence_quotes.quote: This study assessed the challenges and opportunities of bringing low-income communities (LICs) under a sewerage connection within the proposed sewerage network plan by 2025. We conducted nine key-informant interviews from DWASA and City Corporation, and 23 focus-group discussions with landlords, tenants, and Community Based Organisations (CBOs) from 16 LICs near the proposed catchment area.

Landlord/homeowner groups from the four study locations out of sixteen mentioned that the land on which they were residing was owned by the government, and it was repeated in 3 FGDs that they did not have legal registration from the government. Therefore, they remained uncertain about the government granting permission to them to live there, and hence were not taking any initiatives to improve their toilets.

Three key personnel from DWASA, who are also actively engaged in DSIP, mentioned that households within 100 feet of the proposed main sewerage line would be forced to connect with that sewerage network after imposing regulations by concerned authority (i.e., City Corporation or DWASA). They also added that residents of these areas might need to obey this regulation in order to continue their residency.

It has been mentioned in the sewerage master plan that sewerage service fees may be charged up to 2% of the total monthly income of the users based on the services received. Based on all the FGDs, the amount ranges from 50–500 taka monthly.

Participants from 8 LICs asserted that as they were not permanently settled, they were not willing to renovate the existing toilet facilities or even interested to bear any cost of installing the sewerage connection.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community sanitation and sewerage network service access across 16 low-income communities (LICs) in Dhaka under the Dhaka Sanitation Improvement Project (DSIP).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines utility governance, municipal/DWASA planning, and institutional arrangements for extending sewerage to slums. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly empirically examines (1) land tenure, lack of legal registration on government/leased land, and eviction notices governing household/landlord sewerage connection and toilet investment (documentation/tenure requirements), (2) tariff, connection-cost-sharing, and subsidy rules (DWASA uniform tariffs, proposed <=2% income fee cap, income-based/area-based/household-size subsidies, EMI/vouchers) (tariff and cost-recovery rules), and (3) mandatory connection and residency enforcement regulations for households within 100 feet of the main sewer line (enforcement/regulatory rules directly governing connection).
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative empirical study conducted between February 2019 and February 2020 using 9 key informant interviews (DWASA, Dhaka City Corporation, PSTP, ITN-BUET, DSK) and 23 focus group discussions (6-10 participants per FGD) across 16 purposively stratified LICs, analysed via six-phase thematic analysis (open, axial, and selective coding). Per review protocol, qualitative empirical studies of rule-type mechanisms are included in the systematic review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports empirical outcomes on current sanitation and sewerage connection status/exclusion across 16 LICs (e.g., lack of main sewer connections, shared vs. private toilets, reluctance to upgrade toilets without legal registration/tenure) as well as willingness to connect and affordability thresholds for connection installation costs and monthly sewerage tariffs (50-500 BDT/month for tenants; 10-20% of installation cost for landlords).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (landlords, tenants, and CBO leaders in 23 FGDs across 16 LICs in Dhaka South and North City Corporations, plus 9 utility/municipal/NGO key informants), rule-type exposures (unregistered/insecure land tenure, mandatory connection regulations, and tariff/subsidy/cost-sharing rules), outcomes (current sewerage connection/exclusion, willingness to connect/invest, and affordability), and study design (qualitative exploratory KII and FGD study with thematic analysis) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative exploratory study using key informant interviews (n = 9) and focus group discussions (n = 23 across 16 low-income communities) with inductive thematic analysis (open, axial, and selective coding).
population_and_sample: Low-income community (LIC) stakeholders and utility/municipal officials in Dhaka, Bangladesh: 23 focus group discussions (6–10 participants each) with landlords, tenants, and CBO leaders across 16 purposively stratified LICs in Dhaka South and Dhaka North City Corporations, plus 9 key informant interviews with officials from DWASA, Pagla Sewerage Treatment Plant, Dhaka City Corporation, ITN-BUET, and Dushtha Shasthya Kendra (DSK). Units of analysis: LIC settlements, FGD stakeholder groups (landlords, tenants, CBOs), and institutional informants.
exposure: Land tenure and legal registration status (unregistered/illegal settlements on government, leased, or disputed land and eviction notices), mandatory sewer connection residency regulations (within 100 feet of the trunk main), and tariff, connection-fee, and subsidy/cost-recovery rules under DWASA and the Dhaka Sanitation Improvement Project (DSIP).
outcome: Current household/community sewerage connection and sanitation access status across 16 LICs, willingness to connect and invest in toilet/sewer infrastructure, and perceived affordability of sewerage installation costs and monthly service charges.
rationale: Full-text qualitative empirical study examining sewerage network access, exclusion, willingness to connect, and affordability in 16 low-income communities in Dhaka, Bangladesh. It meets all review inclusion criteria (c1–c6), including the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, because it empirically investigates how lack of legal land registration/tenure security and eviction notices deter toilet upgrading and sewer connection investment, alongside mandatory connection/residency enforcement rules (within 100 feet of trunk mains) and tariff, connection-cost-sharing, and pro-poor subsidy structures. Qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies with primary empirical data are eligible for systematic review inclusion.
